body.heading: Verbs tell the time
paragraphs: A verb does more than name an action — it also tells us when the action happens. 'I drink my water' is today. 'I drank my water' already happened. 'I will drink my water' is still to come.

Many verbs make their past by adding -ed, like jump and jumped. But some of the most common verbs in English are rebels: they change their whole shape in the past. Those are the ones worth learning by heart.

body.heading: The rebels: eat, drink, do, go
paragraphs: Eat — I eat an apple today. I ate an apple yesterday. I will eat an apple tomorrow.
Drink — I drink milk today. I drank milk yesterday. I will drink milk tomorrow.
Do — I do my work today. I did my work yesterday. I will do my work tomorrow.
Go — I go to school today. I went to school yesterday. I will go to school tomorrow.

body.heading: More rebels: come, get, make, see, take, give
paragraphs: Come — I come home today. I came home yesterday. I will come home tomorrow.
Get — I get a sticker today. I got a sticker yesterday. I will get a sticker tomorrow.
Make — I make a card today. I made a card yesterday. I will make a card tomorrow.
See — I see a robin today. I saw a robin yesterday. I will see a robin tomorrow.
Take — I take a photo today. I took a photo yesterday. I will take a photo tomorrow.
Give — I give a flower today. I gave a flower yesterday. I will give a flower tomorrow.

body.heading: The easy future
paragraphs: Here is the good news: the future is the same for every verb. Just put will in front and keep the verb as it is — I will go, she will see, they will give. No shape changes, ever.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Tell your day in three sentences: one about yesterday (past), one about right now (present), one about tomorrow (future).
2. Which rebel verb do you think is the strangest — go/went or see/saw? Why?

takeaway: The past tense of common verbs often changes shape completely — drank, ate, went, saw, gave — while the future is always just 'will' plus the verb.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
